question: Explain WHAT IS in Grade 9 Physics (Introduction).
answer: SCIENCE? The knowledge gained through observation and experimentation is termed. as science. The word 'science' has its origin in Latin word 'scientia' which means knowledge. Initially this knowledge was studied under a single heading called 'natural philosophy' because of its limited contents. This situation prevailed till the end of seventeenth century. Industrial revolution took place in the eighteenth century and rapid growth in science and technology was also observed. With the passage of time the volume of knowledge about science increased many folds justifying its division into two main branches i.e., physical sciences and biological sciences. Physical Sciences Physical sciences deal with the study of non-living things. Physical sciences are further divided into main five disciplines i.e., Physics, Chemistry, Astronomy, Geology and Meteorology. These disciplines have no well-defined boundaries and this division is made in order to facilitate scientists for study. Physics is present at the roots of every field of science and provides a picture of the world which is continually changing. Biological Sciences Biological sciences deal with the study of living things. Botany, Zoology and Microbiology are the main disciplines of biological sciences.

question: Explain Branches of Classical Physics Classical in Grade 9 Physics (Introduction).
answer: Physics deals with principles developed in many areas of Physics before 20th century and are given below as branches of classical Physics. Each branch of Physics has become so vast that it can be treated as a separate subject. Mechanics It deals with the study of motion of material objects with or without reference of the forces. Heat / Thermal Physics It deals with the nature of heat, mechanisms of heat transfer and its effects on matter. Thermodynamics It deals with conversion of heat energy into other forms of energy (i.., mechanical, electrical or chemical energy etc.) or vice versa. Optics It deals with the nature, production, propagation of light and phenomena related to it (i.e., reflection, refraction, interference, diffraction and polarization etc.). The working and use of optical instruments such as camera, microscope and telescope etc. is also studied. Electricity and Magnetism / Electromagnetism It deals with the study of the charges which are either at rest or in motion, their effects and their relationship with magnetism. Electromagnetism is the study of phenomena and laws relating electricity and magnetism. Atomic Physics It deals with the study of structure and properties of atoms. Acoustics The branch of Physics that deals with study of sound (i.c., infrasonic, audible sound and ultrasonic), its production, control, propagation, detection and other related phenomena is called acoustics.
subject: Physics

question: Explain Branches of Modern Physics in Grade 9 Physics (Introduction).
answer: The developments made in 20th century are studied under the heading of 'Modern Physics' and its various branches are listed as under. Nuclear Physics: It deals with the study of structure, properties and reactions of nuclei of atoms. Solid State Physics It deals with the study of physical properties of solid materials. It is also called as 'Condensed Matter Physics'. Semiconductor Physics It deals with study, design and use of devices based on behaviour of electrons in semiconductors. Low Temperature Physics It deals with production of extremely low temperature and study of properties of matter at low temperatures. It is also known as 'Cryogenics' derived from the Greek meaning 'producing cold'. Quantum Mechanics It deals with the study of matter, electromagnetic radiation and their interactions based on quantum theory. Particle Physics It deals with the study of elementary particles of the nucleus. Plasma Physics It deals with the study of production and properties of the ionic state of matter i.e., nuclei without electrons. Plasma is also referred as the fourth state of matter.

question: Explain HYPOTHESIS, THEORY AND LAW Hypothesis in Grade 9 Physics (Introduction).
answer: It is defined as the possible explanation of specific observable natural phenomenon based on simplified postulates assumptions or axioms which may be true or untrue. A hypothesis requires further scientific observations and research in order to establish whether the postulates are true or not. The hypothesis may change significantly with more observations. The special theory of relativity is based on two postulates. Bohr model of hydrogen atom is also based on certain postulates. You will study these topics in higher classes. Theory When a hypothesis is tested multiple times with positive results then it is given the name of theory. A theory about a natural phenomenon is more certain than a hypothesis, The atomic theory describes the nature of matter and is supported by experimental evidence. Similarly, the description of large-scale movement of inner layers of the Earth is given by plate tectonic theory. The studies about earthquakes, volcanoes and rocks under sea floor etc. provide evidence about plate tectonic theory. Law A relation among different parameters of a phenomenon which has been found empirically true and applicable in all cases is called a law. The examples are Newton's laws of motion, Newton's law of universal gravitation, Coulomb's law and laws of radioactivity etc.

question: Explain Internationalsystem Of Units in Grade 9 Physics (Physical Quantities).
answer: Measurement of physical quantities is very common in our daily life. If we say that mass of Physics book is 0.2 then it will make sense only if its units are given i.e., 0.2kg. The measurement of a physical quantity will be meaningful only if it is expressed in proper units. In past, different units were used to measure same physical quantities in various countries. For example, the length was expressed in inches, foot, yard and mile etc. In these systems the conversion of bigger units into smaller units or vice versa was quite complicated and time consuming. The need for a universal system of units was realized to facilitate the growing international collaboration and trade. The International System of Units (from the French Le System International of d'Unites, with the internationally accepted abbreviation SI) is the modern version of the metric system. This was recommended by the 11th General Conference of Weights and Measures held in Paris in 1960. This is widely used system of measurements in science, engineering and technology throughout the world. The conversion of bigger units into smaller units is quite simple and straight forward because it involves multiplication or division by ten (10) or powers of ten. The SI system is based on seven base quantities which are given below. (1) Length (2) Mass (3) Time (4) Electric current (5) Temperature (6)Amountofsubstance —_ (7) Intensity of light

question: Explain Scalar Quantity in Grade 9 Physics (Physical Quantities).
answer: A quantity which is completely specified by its magnitude only is called a scalar quantity. There is no need to specify the direction. The examples of scalar quantities include mass, distance, time, temperature, speed, volume, density, work, energy and power etc. The magnitude of such quantity can be expressed by a number with the proper unit. For example, the distance between two points on ground is 20 m. Here 20 represents the magnitude and m is the SI unit of distance. Scalar quantities can be added, subtracted, multiplied or divided by using usual arithmetical laws.

question: Explain Vector Quantity in Grade 9 Physics (Physical Quantities).
answer: A quantity which is completely specified by its magnitude as well as direction is called a vector quantity. You are asked to move five steps. Do you think that this message contains full information? The message is not clear because it does not specify the direction i.e., in the forward, backward, right or left side of the person... However, if direction is mentioned then message is clear. Thus, displacement is a vector quantity. Other examples of vector quantities include velocity, acceleration, force, weight, momentum, torque, electric field and magnetic field etc. A vector quantity becomes meaningful only if its magnitude is expressed by a number with a proper unit and its direction is also specified. Consider an example of a truck which is travelling on a straight flat road which is heading towards North. If the truck travels a distance of 20 km, then 20 km towards North represents its displacement. Similarly, if the weight of an object is 500 N, then it represents a force of 500 N (magnitude) with which the object is attracted by the Earth towards its centre (direction). A vector quantity can be represented by a bold face letter such'as-d (displacement), v (velocity) and F (force) etc. or by an arrow over its symbol _i.e., d, vand F.

question: Explain Significant Figures in Grade 9 Physics (Physical Quantities).
answer: In any measurement, the accurately known digits and the first uncertain or doubtful digit in an expression are called significant figures. For example, the diameter of metallic wire as measured by a micrometer screw gauge is 2.65 mm, then there are three significant figures and the last digit 5 is uncertain or doubtful. The precision of a measured value of a physical quantity is given by significant figures. This is illustrated by the following example. Tf 127 mm and 25 mm represent the length and width of a rectangle, the calculated value of area of the rectangle is 127 x 25 = 3175 mm'. We know that the last digit in cach measurement is uncertain. In other words, length could be anything from 126 mm to 128 mm and width could be anything from 24 mm to 26 mm. Thus, area of rectangle lies between 126 x 24 = 3024 mm' and 128 x 26 = 3328 mm'. The number of significant figures in length are three and number of significant figures in width are two. Thus, the final answer for area should have two significant figures i.e., 3200 mm" or 3.2 x 10° mm', The retaining of the final answer to two significant figures ensures that no additional significant figure is introduced due to multiplication (or division) process. All measurements of physical quantities are subject to uncertainties or errors i.e., they are not accurate or exact. The uncertainty or error denotes the limiting accuracy ofa measurement and depends on the following factors. (a) The quality of the measuring instrument. (b) — The skill of the person using that instrument.

question: Summarize the key points of Kinematics in Grade 9 Physics.
answer: Mechanics is defined as the branch of Physics that deals with the study of forces, motion and their mutual relationship. Mechanics is divided into three parts. (i) Statics (ii) Kinematics (iii) Dynamics The part of mechanics that deals with the study of objects at rest is called statics. The part of mechanics that deals with the study of motion of objects without any reference to the cause of motion is called kinematics. The part of mechanics that deals with the study of motion with the reference of mass and force is called dynamics. A body is said to be at rest if it does not change its position with respect to its surroundings. A body is said to be in motion if it changes its position with respect to its surroundings. Restand motion are relative terms. Ifabody moves alonga line without any vibration or rotation, then its motion said to be translatory motion. Ifthe motion ofa body is ina straight line, it is said to have linear motion. Ifabody moves ina circle, then its motion is called circular motion. Ifabody moves in an irregular manner, then its motion is called random motion. When each point of a body moves around a fixed point or axis, then the motion of this body is called rotatory motion. When a body moves to and fro about its mean position then this type of motion is knownas vibratory motion. * The location ofan object or a point ora place with respect to some reference point called origin is called its position. The length of actual path followed between two points is called the distance between these points.

answer: The force between two objects which are in physical contact with each other is called a contact force. Examples of Contact Forces (i) Friction: Ifa highly polished surface is examined undera powerful microscope, then it shows unevenness of the surface in the form of ups and downs. When a surface tends to move against another surface then these ups and downs of the surfaces are interlocked and give rise a force which opposes their relative motion. This force is called friction and is a contact force. (ii) Air Resistance: It is the resistance or opposition offered by air when an object moves through it. When an object is moving in air the air drag force acts ina direction opposite to that of velocity of object and slows down its motion. The air resistance and the object moving through air are in contact with each other. (iii) Tension: Ifwe suspend an object from one end of the string and hold the other end of string in our hand, then two forces act on the object. Generally, the electric and magnetic effects cannot be separated for the case of a moving charge. When a charged particle is allowed to move in a magnetic field then a force acts on it. question: Explain Energy in Grade 9 Physics (Work, Energy and Power).
answer: Energy is very important concept and frequently used in all sciences. We encounter it quite often in our daily life. We use our muscular energy to perform various activities of life i.e., breathing, talking, walking and running etc. We have to eat food on regular basis to sustain our muscular energy. The compressed spring of toy car has energy stored in it and enables the car to move. Similarly, the running water of a stream or river has energy. Man has been using this energy for centuries to grind food grains in water mill. Almost all natural phenomena are related to energy and its change. The energy of an object is defined as its capacity to do work. Energy is a scalar quantity and measured in joules. Energy exists in a variety of different forms. The various forms of energy include mechanical energy, chemical energy, thermal energy, solar energy, sound energy, electrical energy, magnetic energy and nuclear energy etc.

One or more atoms of same or different elements combine to form a molecule. Matter exists in three states i.e., solid, liquid and gas. Matter can change its state on heating or cooling. For example, ice (the solid form of water) will convert into liquid form ie., water on heating. Further heating of water will convert it into steam which is the gaseous form of water. Similarly, the gaseous form of water i.e., steam can be transformed into its liquid form on cooling. Further cooling will transform the water into its solid form ice. Pressure can also change the state of matter. Gases can be liquified under high pressure. The existence of matter i.e., solid, liquid and gas may be explained on the basis of the particle theory of matter.

Smaller the separation between the particles, the greater will be the force of attraction between them.

If the temperature difference between these two junctions exists, then an e.m.f. ofa few millivolt can be obtained. It is measured by a device attached with the thermocouple.; For example, let one wire is of bismuth and the other one is the antimony. If the one junction is placed in melting ice of temperature 0°C and the other one is at temperature 100°C then an e.m.f. of about 10mV is produced for a temperature difference of 100°C. If the temperature of both the junction is same, equal and opposite e.m.f. will be produced at both junctions and the resultant current flowing through the junction is zero. Thermocouple are widely used in science and industry. Their applications include temperature measurement for furnaces, gas turbine exhaust, diesel engines, and other industrial processes. question: Explain Physics of Solids in Grade 12 Physics.
answer: INTRODUCTION Basically, there are three states of matter solids, liquids and gas. The liquidand gas are compressible and have ability to flow, whereas, solids are incompressible and have definite volume and shapes. These are due to the closeness of their atoms or, molecules. Similarly, there are several kinds of solids, among these, each of them has its different characteristics and properties. Some solids are crystalline while others are amorphous or polymer, some are elastic while others are rigid, some are brittle while others are plastic or ductile, some have electrical conductivity while others have magnetic conductivity. For example, diamond is hard, lead is soft, steal is strong, glass is weak, copper has electrical conductivity and iron has magnetic conductivity. Many solids can be deformed in the form of change in their length, volume or shape by a deforming force. These deformations can be studied in terms of stress and strain.: In this unit we will explain classification of solids. For example, there are three classes of solids with respect to their structure, named as: crystalline, amorphous and polymer. Electrically, there are three classes of solids such as: insulators, conductors and semi-conductors, these can be studied using band theory of solids. Magnetically, the three types of solids are paramagnetic, diamagnetic and ferromagnetic. In addition to the magnetic classes, we will also discuss the phenomenon of hysteresis and hysteresis loop by magnetizing and demagnetizing the magnetic materials.

answer: An amplifier is an electronic circuit which converts.a small input A.C. signal into a large output A.C. signal under the action of a transistor. The amplification takes place under the following three configurations ie., common base amplifier, common emitter amplifier and common collector amplifier, but common emitter amplifier is used mostly. The emitter-base junction is forward biased by using a battery Vas and a resistor Rx called base or input resistor, whereas collector is reverse biased by using another battery Vcc through a resistor Rc known as collector or load resistor. The input A.C. signal is applied in the base and emitter section of the circuit. And the output signal is taken out from the collector-emitter section. In the absence of any input signal, the transistor is working in its normal mode. Now when an A.C. signal is applied at the input terminals of the circuit, then during the positive half cycle of the signal, the base of the transistor which acts as driven element becomes more Positive and it increases the forward biasing across the emitter-base junction. Therefore, more electrons flow from the emitter to the collector through the base and it causes of an increase collector current Ic by f times the input base current Ip (1, =B1, ).
